author: callum_reid
body: Hot take that shouldn't be hot: most AI features shipped this year are a search box with extra steps. Useful? Sometimes. Revolutionary? Mine just autocompleted a calendar invite to 'Meeting with Meeting'.

author: callum_reid
body: Unpopular in my circles: four-day weeks work brilliantly for teams that already had their act together, and expose everyone else within a month. The schedule isn't the fix. It's the X-ray.

author: callum_reid
body: Every startup I've advised that died, died of the same thing: building for the investor deck instead of the person who'd actually use it.

author: callum_reid
body:
Things I wish someone had told me before my first startup:

1. Your first ten customers will teach you more than your first ten hires.
2. 'We'll fix it later' is a loan, and the interest rate is brutal.
3. Busy is not the same as progress, and you can't tell the difference from inside.
4. Pay people properly from day one, even if it means fewer of them.
5. Sleep. I'm serious. Half my worst decisions were made after 1am.

author: callum_reid
body: Remember when 'the cloud' meant someone else's computer? It still does.

author: callum_reid
body: If your company needs a 40-slide deck to explain its culture, the culture is the 40 slides.

author: callum_reid
body: The tram extension took forever, dug up half of Leith Walk and cost a fortune, and I still think building it was right. Big infrastructure always looks like a mistake halfway through. Ask anyone who lived through the Forth bridges going up.

author: callum_reid
body: Hiring advice for developers: I care far less about which framework you know than whether you can explain a bug you caused without blaming the compiler.

author: callum_reid
body:
Deleted every social app from my phone for a week.
Day 1: twitchy.
Day 3: read a whole book.
Day 6: reinstalled one 'just to check something'.
Day 7: here we are.

author: callum_reid
body: The remote work debate is mostly people describing their own flat. Big flat, quiet street, no kids: remote is paradise. Shared flat in Gorgie with a flatmate who drums: the office is a sanctuary.

author: callum_reid
body: Open-source maintainers hold up half the internet for free and we treat them like a vending machine. If your company depends on a library, put some money in the jar.

author: callum_reid
body: Watched my first full cricket match. Still don't know who won. Loved it.

author: callum_reid
body: Hustle culture is just unpaid overtime with a better soundtrack. Do great work, then go home.

author: priya_n
body: Adulthood is realising the 'proper' lunch you're saving the nice bowl for is never coming. Use the nice bowl. Use it for toast.

author: priya_n
body: Small thing I started this year: when a friend comes to mind, I text them right then, no matter how random. 'Saw a dog that looked like your dad.' 'Thinking about that terrible hostel in Lisbon.' Half the time they reply within a minute and we talk for an hour. The other half they reply three days later. Either way the friendship gets a little warmer. It costs nothing and it's the best habit I have.

author: priya_n
body: Reread a novel I loved at nineteen. It's the same book. I'm not the same reader. Lines that made me cry now make me want to shake the narrator and tell her to get a job.

author: priya_n
body: The best part of any party is the twenty minutes in the kitchen with whoever else is avoiding the party.

author: priya_n
body: Asking for a raise got easier when I stopped treating it like a confession and started treating it like an invoice. Here's what I did, here's what it's worth. Shaking hands still optional.

author: priya_n
body: Went to a poetry reading where the poet stopped halfway through to say 'actually this one's not finished' and read the rest anyway. Most honest thing I've seen on a stage all year.

author: priya_n
body: I've stopped saying 'I was so bad, I skipped the gym'. The moral language around exercise made me do less of it, not more. Now I just say I went for a walk instead. Shocking how much easier that is.

author: priya_n
body: Every flat in Edinburgh has one window that simply will not close properly.

author: priya_n
body: My mum's rule: never trust a recipe that says 'season to taste' and then gives exact grams for everything else. Pick a lane.

author: priya_n
body: The train between Edinburgh and Glasgow: under an hour to go from 'what a lovely city' to 'what a lovely different city', arguing about which is better the whole way.

author: priya_n
body: If a film needs three hours, fine. But most films that run three hours needed two and a half and an editor with courage.

author: priya_n
body: Started keeping a list of things that went fine. Not great, just fine. The bus came. The soup was hot. The email didn't need a reply. Turns out most days are mostly fine.

author: sofia_m
body: Coaching rule I'll die on: under-10s should never see a league table. They should see a ball, a lot of it, and as many touches as we can give them.

author: sofia_m
body: Strength training isn't only for people who want to look a certain way. It's for the version of you at 75 who wants to get up off the floor without help. Train for her.

author: sofia_m
body: Women's football crowds here have grown so much since I arrived, and nobody I coach finds that remarkable, which is the most remarkable part. My under-12 girls don't know that at their age I was the only girl on a boys' team, and parents on the touchline shouted at the ref to 'let the lads play'. They just assume there's a pitch and a kit and a coach for them. Good. That's what progress feels like: boring.

author: sofia_m
body: Rest days aren't lazy days. A lot of the adapting happens while you recover, not while you lift. Your sofa is part of the programme.

author: sofia_m
body: VAR has made football fairer and less fun, and I genuinely don't know which matters more.

author: sofia_m
body: Tried cold water swimming at Portobello because everyone said it would change my life. It changed my opinion of my own toes. I'll go again, though. The tea afterwards is unmatched.

author: sofia_m
body: Penalty shootouts are a coin toss with extra crying. Change my mind.

author: sofia_m
body: Coached a seven-year-old today who scored, then ran back to apologise to the goalkeeper. I didn't have the heart to correct her.

author: sofia_m
body: Every council that sells off a playing field 'because it's underused' should have to explain where the next generation of players is meant to come from. Fields don't come back.

author: sofia_m
body: Hot take from a coach: most adults don't need a fancy programme. Walk more, lift something heavy twice a week, sleep like it's your job. Everything else is decoration.

author: sofia_m
body: Saturday morning reminder: the parents shouting loudest on the touchline are rarely the ones who've played. Let the kids enjoy it.

author: dami
body: Thursday supper club menu: jollof, smoked mackerel, pickled red onions, and cranachan with a little uda pepper in the cream. Twelve strangers came in, twelve friends left. That's the whole business model.

author: dami
body: The great jollof debate is settled and I'm not telling you which side won, because I want to keep my Ghanaian friends.

author: dami
body: Leith on a sunny Saturday is a different country from Leith on a wet Tuesday, and I love both for opposite reasons.

author: dami
body: A small rant about 'authentic'. People ask if my food is authentic and I never know what they want. My grandmother in Ibadan cooked with whatever the market had that week. My mum in Peckham cooked with whatever the big supermarket had that week. I cook in Leith with whatever the fishmonger on the corner has. Every one of us was authentic. The only inauthentic cooking is cooking to impress someone who isn't at the table.

author: dami
body: Rice-to-water ratios are a personality test and I've stopped arguing about them at dinner.

author: dami
body: Small food businesses are being squeezed off our high streets while units sit empty for years waiting for a rent nobody local can pay. Nobody voted for that. It just happened while we were looking at something else.

author: dami
body: Scotch bonnet tip: wear gloves. Learn from my Tuesday.

author: dami
body: Underrated Edinburgh: the Water of Leith walk from Dean Village to Stockbridge on a weekday morning. Herons, joggers, and one man who sings to the ducks.

author: dami
body: Running a supper club pays like a hobby and takes hours like a job. Still the best decision I've made. But I'd be lying if I said the maths works without a day job.

author: dami
body: Cookbooks are the most underrated memoirs. You learn who someone fed, what they could afford, and what they missed from home.

author: dami
body: Friendly reminder that frozen peas are a vegetable, not a moral failure.

author: dami
body: First time in Aberdeen. Granite everywhere, and when the sun comes out it bounces off every wall like a disco. Everyone told me it was grey. It sparkles.

author: hugo_lb
body: That huge moon on the horizon last night wasn't actually bigger. It's an illusion: your brain compares it to roofs and trees and decides it must be enormous. Hold your thumb up next time. Same size as when it's high.

author: hugo_lb
body: Why is the sky blue but sunsets red? Sunlight is a mix of colours. Air molecules scatter short wavelengths, like blue, much more than long ones, like red. At midday the light comes down through a fairly thin slice of air, and the scattered blue fills the sky. At sunset the light skims through far more atmosphere, most of the blue is scattered away before it reaches you, and what's left is orange and red. Same physics, different angle.

author: hugo_lb
body: Astronomy is the only science where the main lab equipment is patience and a thermos.

author: hugo_lb
body: Every time someone says 'AI will replace scientists', I think of my old supervisor spending three weeks discovering that a telescope glitch was a moth. Good luck automating the moth.

author: hugo_lb
body: Pub fact: if you could fold a sheet of paper in half 42 times, it would be thick enough to reach the Moon. You can't, of course. You'll manage seven, maybe eight, and then argue about technique.

author: hugo_lb
body: Science communication tip: if you can't explain your research to a twelve-year-old, you might not understand it. If you can't explain it to a twelve-year-old in under a minute, that's fine. They have other plans.

author: hugo_lb
body: If you want properly dark skies without leaving Scotland, Galloway Forest is extraordinary. On a clear night the Milky Way looks like someone spilled a drink across the sky.

author: hugo_lb
body: Peer review is a terrible system, except for all the others. It catches some errors, misses others, and occasionally waves a confident mistake through. Treat a single paper like a single witness.

author: hugo_lb
body: A big cumulus cloud weighs about as much as a herd of elephants. It's floating over your bus stop right now.

author: hugo_lb
body: Aurora forecasts are weather forecasts for the sky's mood. 'Strong activity tonight' means 'maybe, if the clouds cooperate', and in Scotland the clouds never cooperate. Still: look north after ten.

author: hugo_lb
body: Science fiction that gets the physics wrong but the people right will always beat the reverse.

author: hugo_lb
body: Teaching my dad to use a password manager. He has now asked me what the password to the password manager is. Fair question, honestly.

author: tomas
body: The lab replicated last spring's result, at half the effect size. That's still worth knowing.

author: tomas
body: Nobody writes a paper titled 'We checked and it was fine'. Somebody should. I'd read it twice.

author: tomas
body: Three weeks chasing a contamination problem in our cell cultures. We changed the media, the incubator, the hoods, our gloves. It turned out to be one bottle of buffer that someone had been topping up instead of replacing. Nobody will ever publish this, but every lab tech reading just nodded. Half of science is boring detective work that makes the exciting result possible. The other half is labelling things properly so the next person doesn't have to do the detective work.

author: tomas
body: Pipettes should come with a little counter, like a step counter. I'd like to know how many times I've pressed this button in my life. My thumb would also like to know.

author: tomas
body: The lab radio has played the same four songs since August.

author: tomas
body: Lab techs are paid less than almost anyone in the building and know where absolutely everything is. If you want your research to happen, be nice to us.

author: tomas
body: Lab rule: the fridge with the biohazard sticker is not the lunch fridge. We've had to say this out loud twice this month.

author: rin
body: Usability test today. A participant spent four minutes looking for the save button, which the design team had turned into a tasteful grey cloud icon. He thought it was the weather.

author: rin
body: Dark patterns are a choice. Every 'Are you sure you want to miss out?' button was argued about in a meeting, and someone lost.

author: rin
body: Glasgow taught me to talk to strangers at bus stops. Edinburgh is teaching me to stop. I'm somewhere in the middle, nodding at people very intensely.

author: rin
body: Watched a Japanese film in a tiny cinema in Tollcross. The subtitles translated every polite phrase as 'OK'. The audience laughed at all the wrong moments and honestly, they were right to.

author: rin
body: Something I keep telling product teams: users don't read. Not because they're lazy, because they're busy. They scan for the one word that matches what they came to do. If that word is 'Proceed' and they came to pay, they hesitate. If it's 'Continue' and they came to cancel, they panic. Half my job is replacing clever words with obvious ones and watching the success rate climb. Nobody gets promoted for writing 'Pay now', but they should.

author: rin
body: My umbrella has been to more countries than most people I know.

author: rin
body: Friends from Osaka visiting next month. They want castles, whisky and 'the wizard café'. I'm taking them to a chippy in Portobello and up a hill in the rain. They will thank me later.

author: ailsa_m
body: Taught my P4 class a Gaelic song about a seal. Now three of them answer the register by barking. Language revival takes many forms.

author: ailsa_m
body: If you've only seen Lewis in photos on a sunny day, you've seen a lie. A beautiful lie. Come in November and meet the real island, sideways rain and all.

author: ailsa_m
body: Gaelic-medium education gets framed as either a heritage hobby or a waste of money, and I'd gently say it's neither. Kids who grow up bilingual aren't doing it for a museum. They're doing it because it's the language their granny speaks to them on the phone, and the language half the place names around them are in. Funding it isn't nostalgia. It's deciding a living language gets to keep living. Happy to hear disagreement, but visit a classroom first.

author: ailsa_m
body: Research I keep coming back to: bilingual kids aren't confused by two languages. They mix them while they're learning, the way adults mix up words when they're tired. The mixing is part of the learning.

author: ailsa_m
body: Gaelic has no single word for 'yes'. Teaching that to six-year-olds is a delight.

author: ailsa_m
body: Ferry from Ullapool cancelled again. Third time this month. My mum has stopped saying 'see you Friday' and started saying 'see you when the sea allows'.

author: kwame_o
body: A&E tip from someone who works there: bring a phone charger, a list of your medications and a snack. You'll thank me around hour three.

author: kwame_o
body: Things people apologise to me for in A&E: wasting my time, swearing when the needle goes in, their socks. The people who worry they're wasting my time almost never are.

author: kwame_o
body: On wellness influencers: I don't mind people selling smoothies. I mind when the pitch is that your doctor is hiding something from you. I'm not. I'm hiding nothing, mostly because I haven't had time to eat since breakfast. If a supplement or routine makes you feel good and your GP is happy with it, great. Just be suspicious of anyone whose advice comes with a discount code and a villain. Real medicine is boring and mostly says 'it depends'.

author: kwame_o
body: View from the frontline: we don't need another restructure. We need enough beds, enough staff and a printer that works. In that order. Possibly printer first.

author: kwame_o
body: Night shift brain: I just put the milk in the cupboard and the cereal in the fridge.

author: kwame_o
body: If you've been taking painkillers every day for weeks to get through, that's worth a conversation with a GP or pharmacist, not a secret. Nobody will tell you off. We'd just rather know.

author: kwame_o
body: Growing up supporting Aberdeen taught me resilience, patience, and how to find something positive about a 0-0 in February.

author: kwame_o
body: Sleep after a night shift isn't real sleep. It's a hostage negotiation with daylight and the neighbour's drill.

author: lena_k
body: Night bus confession: four Saturdays in a row I have driven past a man in a full wedding suit, alone, eating chips at 3am. I have never asked. I don't want to know. I want the mystery.

author: lena_k
body: Free bus travel for under-22s is the best thing this country has done in years, and I say that as the person who has to tell them to take their feet off the seats.

author: lena_k
body: Shift patterns for bus drivers are designed by someone who has never had to find a toilet at 2am on the edge of town.

author: lena_k
body: Everyone wants more buses and nobody wants a bus lane outside their house. I understand. But the bus can't fly.

author: lena_k
body: Best view in the city: top deck, front seat, coming down the Mound at dusk. Free with a bus pass. You're welcome.

author: lena_k
body: Saw the northern lights from the depot car park last month, faint green over the Pentlands. Twenty years of night shifts and that was the first time. Worth the wait.

author: lena_k
body: To the lady who says 'thank you, driver' every single night: you're why I keep going.

author: marco_b
body: Pineapple on pizza: I don't like it, I won't make it, and I've stopped being angry about it. It's your pizza. It's my oven. We can coexist.

author: marco_b
body: People ask why my dough rests for 48 hours. Because that's how long it takes to become good. Flour, water, salt, a tiny bit of yeast, time. Time is the ingredient nobody wants to pay for. Every shortcut makes a pizza that's fine. Fine is not why I left Naples, carried a starter through airport security in a jam jar, and explained to a very confused officer that it was 'family'. Fine is not why I get up at six.

author: marco_b
body: Real Neapolitan pizza is soft in the middle. It's meant to be. If you want crunchy, get a cracker. With love.

author: marco_b
body: Eleven years in Scotland and I still put on a coat in June and feel personally betrayed.

author: marco_b
body: Tinned tomatoes beat fresh ones for sauce nine months of the year. Fight me.

author: marco_b
body: Napoli winning the league was the happiest week of my life after my daughter being born. My wife says this is not something you say out loud. I'm saying it out loud.

author: marco_b
body: Put a tiny bit of anchovy in your tomato sauce. Nobody will taste fish. Everybody will taste 'why is this so good'.

author: fatima_z
body: Low traffic neighbourhoods are the most heated topic in my inbox, so here's my honest view as a planner. They work best when they're designed with the people who live there, not dropped on them over a summer. The street gets quieter, kids walk to school, local shops often do fine or better. But if your elderly mum's carer now needs twelve extra minutes to reach her, that's a real cost, not a whinge. Good schemes listen and adjust. Bad ones treat every complaint as backlash.

author: fatima_z
body: Edinburgh's closes are the best urban design accident in Europe. Narrow, steep, a bit dark, and they turn every walk into a choose-your-own-adventure.

author: fatima_z
body: Benches are political. When a city removes them 'to stop loitering', it also removes them from the pensioner who needs a sit-down halfway up the hill.

author: fatima_z
body: Cycled to work all of last winter. I'm not fitter, exactly, but I'm a lot less grumpy. My colleagues confirm this.

author: fatima_z
body: Housing is the issue underneath every other issue in this city. Transport, schools, the festival, whether a nurse can afford to live near the hospital. Pull any thread and it leads back to rent.

author: fatima_z
body: Lyon has traboules, Edinburgh has closes. Both cities built secret shortcuts through their buildings and both are now extremely proud of it.

author: fatima_z
body: Bike stolen. Third one. I'm starting to take it personally.

author: ollie_p
body: Derby day. If you need me I'll be in the East Stand doing the breathing exercises my wife found on the internet.

author: ollie_p
body: We drew. I've aged ten years. Same time next season.

author: ollie_p
body: Plumbing physics nobody tells you: water expands when it freezes, so a pipe in an unheated loft can split in one cold night. Lag your pipes before the first frost, not after the ceiling comes in.

author: ollie_p
body: Ten years self-employed, here's the honest version. Good bits: nobody tells me when to have lunch, I meet hundreds of people, and fixing someone's boiler on a freezing morning gets you a kind of thanks you never get in an office. Bad bits: no sick pay, chasing invoices like a bailiff, and every January people decide plumbers should cost less. If you're thinking about a trade, do it, but learn the paperwork as seriously as the pipes.

author: ollie_p
body: Unpopular in my house: the top flight here needs more teams, not fewer. More derbies, fewer seasons of playing the same side four times.

author: ollie_p
body: A customer offered me a cup of tea, a biscuit, a slice of cake and then her late husband's toolbox. I said no to the toolbox. I'm still thinking about it.

author: ollie_p
body: A pie at the football isn't food, it's a ritual. You don't eat it for the taste. You eat it so you've got something to do with your hands at half time.

author: ollie_p
body: Hibs fans, I love you, but booing our own team at 0-0 in the 60th minute has never once helped them score.

author: ines_r
body: A model with 95% accuracy can still be useless. If 95% of your emails aren't spam, a model that says 'not spam' every single time is 95% accurate and catches nothing. I say this in every meeting and I get the same face every time: polite horror, then a request for a new slide. Accuracy is a number. Whether it helps is a question. Please ask the question.

author: ines_r
body: AI isn't going to take your job. A manager who's read one article about AI might, though.

author: ines_r
body: Every dataset is a photograph of the past. If the past was unfair, the model learns to be unfair with excellent precision.

author: ines_r
body: Correlation isn't causation, but it isn't nothing either. It's a raised eyebrow. Follow the eyebrow, carefully.

author: ines_r
body: Lisbon taught me that a city can be beautiful and unaffordable for the people who make it beautiful. Edinburgh, please take notes.

author: ines_r
body: My model is overfitting. So am I, to this sofa.

author: ines_r
body: Portuguese people in Scotland, how do you survive without proper custard tarts? I've tried six bakeries. Kind attempts, all of them. None of them right.

author: dev_s
body: Saved for a house deposit for six years. In four of them, prices rose faster than my savings did. The maths of 'just save harder' has changed and nobody updated the advice.

author: dev_s
body: Your card got declined abroad because a fraud model saw 'coffee in Lisbon at 7am' and decided you were a criminal. It wasn't wrong to be suspicious. You were a little suspicious.

author: dev_s
body: My view after years in payments: crypto isn't the future of money and it isn't purely a scam either. It behaves like a speculative asset with a fan club. Treat it like that and you'll sleep fine.

author: dev_s
body: Payment systems are held together by a surprising amount of overnight batch processing, files sent between banks on a schedule, and engineers who are very, very nervous about bank holidays. When you tap your card it feels instant. The authorisation is. Actually moving the money often isn't. If you've ever wondered why a refund takes five days, it's because somewhere a file is waiting for the right moment to leave.

author: dev_s
body: Pension contributions are boring. That's how you know they're working.

author: dev_s
body: Made my mum's dal over video call. She watched the whole thing and said 'too much water' four times. She was right four times.

author: niamh_c
body: Nurse tip: if a relative is in hospital, write your questions down before the ward round. Doctors move fast, and everyone forgets their question the second someone asks 'any questions?'

author: niamh_c
body: Fourteen years nursing, and the thing that might make me leave isn't the workload. It's the car park. Paying to park at your own workplace, at 7pm, for a twelve-hour shift, in the rain, after walking past three empty spaces reserved for people who left at four. I know it's a small thing. Small things are what you can't stop thinking about at 4am with a cold coffee. Fix the small things and you keep the people.

author: niamh_c
body: Hand hygiene posters have been on every hospital wall for twenty years and they still matter. Boring public health is still public health.

author: niamh_c
body: Nurses striking isn't nurses abandoning patients. It's nurses saying we can't keep doing this and keep it safe. You can disagree with the decision, but please don't call it selfish.

author: niamh_c
body: Drink water. Wear sunscreen. Go to your smear test. Thank you.

author: niamh_c
body: Galway to Edinburgh: same rain, different accent, more hills. My calves are furious.

author: niamh_c
body: Night shifts change how you see the hours. 3am is the loneliest. 5am is the most hopeful. Something about the light and the tea trolley.

author: bjorn_e
body: People ask what an ice core actually tells you. As snow gets buried and squeezed into ice, it traps tiny bubbles of air, so you're literally looking at samples of the atmosphere from thousands of years ago. In some places you can count the yearly layers like tree rings. When I hold a section that fell as snow before anyone had written anything down, I still go a bit quiet. It's the closest thing to time travel I'll ever do.

author: bjorn_e
body: Climate models aren't crystal balls. They're very careful 'if this, then probably that' machines. The 'if' is the part we still control.

author: bjorn_e
body: I'm a climate scientist and I drive a car. I also eat meat twice a week. Purity tests make for great arguments and terrible coalitions.

author: bjorn_e
body: Ice core lab: minus twenty. My office: also, somehow, minus twenty.

author: bjorn_e
body: Sauna update: found one in Portobello that heats properly and lets you run straight into the sea afterwards. I have found my Edinburgh home.

author: bjorn_e
body: Glaciers don't retreat in a neat straight line. Some hang on for years and then lose a lot very quickly. A bit like a friend who seems fine until suddenly they aren't.

author: chen_wei
body: My robot can open a door 60% of the time. The other 40% it bows to the door politely and gives up. Honestly relatable.

author: chen_wei
body: Robot demo videos are always sped up four times with upbeat music. Real robotics research is a person sitting very still, watching a gripper fail to pick up a sock for an hour.

author: chen_wei
body: Moravec's paradox in one sentence: the things a toddler finds easy, like picking up a toy, are the hard part for a robot. Chess was easy. Laundry is the frontier.

author: chen_wei
body: Found a hand-pulled noodle place near the university that tastes like Xi'an. I won't name it. I need it to not have a queue.

author: chen_wei
body: Battery life is the real boss of robotics. Everything else is negotiation.

author: chen_wei
body: Robots trained only in simulation are like people who learned to swim from a book. Everything is perfect until the first wave.

author: yasmin_a
body: Tax return reminder: keep your receipts in one place. Not a shoebox. Not the glovebox. Not your 'I'll sort it later' email folder. One place. Your future self is begging you.

author: yasmin_a
body: The question I get most as an accountant isn't about tax, it's 'is this normal?'. Is it normal to have no savings at 30? Is it normal to dread opening your banking app? Is it normal to earn decently and still feel broke? Mostly yes, and the shame makes it worse. The people who do best with money aren't the ones who know the most. They're the ones who look at it regularly without flinching. Start by looking.

author: yasmin_a
body: Club cricket in Scotland is the purest sport there is. Three people watching, one of them a dog, rain stops play twice, and everyone stays for the tea.

author: yasmin_a
body: Side hustles are fine. Turning every hobby into a side hustle until you have no hobbies left is a different thing.

author: yasmin_a
body: Scotland's cricket team deserves far more attention than it gets. They've beaten bigger sides than you'd think, and most people here couldn't tell you when the next fixture is.

author: yasmin_a
body: Budgets are just plans that admit they might be wrong.

author: yasmin_a
body: My Glaswegian dad visited Edinburgh, complained about the prices, the hills and the wind, then said 'it's quite nice, though' on the train home. High praise.

author: lucas_f
body: Jiu-jitsu is a sport where a small person can choke a big person and everyone shakes hands afterwards. Best therapy I know.

author: lucas_f
body: Coffee confession: back home most people I know drink it sweet, strong-ish and in tiny cups, all day long. Then I moved here and paid four pounds for a flat white the size of a soup bowl. Both are correct.

author: lucas_f
body: Ego is the most common injury in a jiu-jitsu gym. Tap early. Tap often. Come back tomorrow.

author: lucas_f
body: Brought pão de queijo to the gym after class. Nobody complained.

author: lucas_f
body: Friends in Rio ask what Edinburgh is like. I tell them: imagine a castle, a volcano, a lot of wind, and people who apologise when you bump into them.

author: lucas_f
body: Martial arts belts should take longer, not shorter. The waiting teaches more than the technique.

author: eilidh
body: Four Fringe shows in, here's what I've learned. You will flyer for six hours in the rain and get two people. One of them will be your aunt. The other will be a stranger who laughs at the one joke nobody else gets and comes back the next night with friends. You do the whole festival for that stranger. Also, pack more socks than you think. Wet feet are where dreams go to die.

author: eilidh
body: Edinburgh in August is the best and worst city in the world at the same time, and I've never managed to explain it to anyone who hasn't lived through one.

author: eilidh
body: Artist pricing is a nightmare. If I charge what a commission is worth, people gasp. If I charge what they expect, I eat beans for a month. The beans are fine, though.

author: eilidh
body: Drawing the city on the back of receipts started as a joke. Now I have about 300 of them and a café in Bruntsfield wants to put them on the wall. Life is strange.

author: eilidh
body: AI art isn't art. It's a very fast collage of other people's work.

author: eilidh
body: Overheard on the Royal Mile: 'Is the castle open on Sundays, or is it a religious castle?'

author: eilidh
body: Comics deserve more shelf space in libraries. Some of the best writing I've read this year came in speech bubbles.

author: sam_okafor
body: Rent controls are popular for understandable reasons, so I want to be honest about why I'm wary. In most of the studies I've read, hard caps help sitting tenants in the short run and reduce how many homes get built or let over time. That's not an argument for doing nothing. It's an argument that a cap alone won't fix supply. Build more, protect tenants from sudden hikes, tax empty homes. Boring answer, I know. Boring answers are my whole career.

author: sam_okafor
body: GDP is a decent measure of how much stuff a country makes and a poor measure of whether the people in it are OK.

author: sam_okafor
body: Universal basic income: I think it's worth piloting properly. Not because I'm sure it works, but because we've spent a decade arguing about it with almost no good local data.

author: sam_okafor
body: Inflation feels personal because it is. The average doesn't care that your particular basket is mostly bread, rent and bus fares.

author: sam_okafor
body: Every policy has a trade-off. If someone tells you theirs doesn't, ask again.

author: sam_okafor
body: Jollof debate update: I'm Nigerian, I'm an economist, and I can confirm the evidence is overwhelming. Nigerian. Peer review welcome.

author: sam_okafor
body: Most of the evidence I've read suggests moderate minimum wage rises haven't destroyed jobs the way people feared in the 90s. They aren't free, either. The research is boring and fairly reassuring, which is why nobody quotes it.

author: sam_okafor
body: Local elections decide your bins, your libraries and your bus routes, and turnout is often dismal. If you want to change something you'll actually notice, that's the vote.

author: anya_h
body: Favourite bug report this year: 'The app works perfectly unless you use it.'

author: anya_h
body: Testers are the people who ask 'what if the user types a name with an apostrophe?' and get looked at like we're being difficult. Then a customer called O'Brien can't log in for three days. Then we're asked why we didn't catch it. We did. It's in the ticket from March, marked 'won't fix, edge case'. Every edge case is somebody's whole name.

author: anya_h
body: Two years in Edinburgh now. People ask if I'll go back to Kharkiv. I say yes, when I can, and they look sad, and I don't know how to explain that it's a happy answer.

author: anya_h
body: Scottish people say 'it's a bit fresh' when it's minus four. I respect the lie.

author: anya_h
body: Went to my first ceilidh. Nobody knew the steps, a man in a kilt shouted instructions, and half the room spun the wrong way. Nobody cared. I've decided this is the national philosophy.

author: pablo_g
body: A guest asked me where to see the Loch Ness Monster 'today, before dinner'. I gave him a bus timetable and a hug.

author: pablo_g
body: Things I've learned running a hostel. Australians will hike anything. Germans will read the house rules, then suggest improvements. Americans will tell you their family tree within ten minutes and somehow it includes a Scottish castle. Spanish guests, my people, will cook dinner at 10pm and invite the whole dorm. And everyone, every single nationality, leaves one sock behind. We have a box. It's enormous.

author: pablo_g
body: The visitor levy is coming and I'm torn. Hostels run on tiny margins and our guests are the ones counting every pound. But the city does need money to cope with August. I'll support it if it's spent where visitors actually go.

author: pablo_g
body: Day trip tip for visitors: skip one Highland coach tour and take the train to North Berwick. Beach, seabirds, a ruined castle, chips. Back by six.

author: pablo_g
body: Spanish breakfast: coffee and toast with tomato. Scottish breakfast: everything that has ever lived. I'm learning to respect both.

author: pablo_g
body: Hospitality wages in this city are not enough to live in this city. That's the sentence. Everything else is detail.

author: pablo_g
body: Guest of the week: a Finnish man who swam at Portobello in October and called it 'refreshing, almost warm'.

author: mei_l
body: Pharmacist PSA: antibiotics won't help a cold. Colds are caused by viruses and antibiotics work on bacteria. I'm not being stingy, I'm being accurate.

author: mei_l
body: The pharmacy counter is the most underrated bit of the health service. We can help with a lot of minor things, tell you whether you actually need a GP, and check your medicines don't argue with each other. Last week a man came in for cough mixture and it turned out two of his prescriptions shouldn't be taken together. Nobody else had caught it. That's a normal Tuesday. Ask your pharmacist. We don't bite, we're just behind a counter.

author: mei_l
body: Drug names are secretly organised. The ending often tells you the family: -olol for beta blockers, -statin for statins, -cillin for penicillins. Once you see it you can't stop.

author: mei_l
body: Supplements aren't magic and they aren't always harmless. Some interact with prescriptions. If you take anything regularly, tell your pharmacist, even if it came from a health food shop.

author: mei_l
body: Bubble tea is a drink and a snack and I will hear no arguments.

author: mei_l
body: The daylight is going and my mood is going with it. Every October I promise myself a lunchtime walk, and every October it's the first thing I drop. Not this year.

author: jakub_n
body: What people get wrong about lager: it's not the boring beer. A properly made Czech lager takes weeks of cold conditioning and has nothing to hide behind. No big hops to cover mistakes. If it's flat or buttery, everyone can taste it. Brewing a great one is like cooking a perfect plain omelette: people think it's easy until they try. I'm proud to brew it in Leith, even if half my customers ask for 'something hoppier'.

author: jakub_n
body: Hazy IPA fans, I love you, but at some point it stopped being beer and became fruit juice with paperwork.

author: jakub_n
body: Friends in Prague asked what Edinburgh is like. I said: more hills, fewer trams, the same number of people asking the way to the castle.

author: jakub_n
body: Beer foam is not a mistake. It's a hat. Respect the hat.

author: jakub_n
body: Ice hockey on a Saturday night is the most Czech I've felt in years. Loud, cold, beer in a plastic cup. Perfect.

author: jakub_n
body: Brewer's tip: the best beer is the one you drink with someone you haven't seen in ages. The second best is whatever's on our second tap.

author: hannah_w
body: Asked my first-years whether it's ever OK to lie. Twenty minutes of debate, then one student said 'only to protect a surprise party'. Kant in shambles.

author: hannah_w
body: Recommendation algorithms aren't neutral. Every one makes a choice about what you should see next, and that choice is usually 'whatever keeps you here'. That's not evil, it's a design goal. But it means your feed is shaped by somebody's metric, and the metric doesn't know you have an essay due. I'd like platforms to say plainly what they optimise for. If the answer is 'your time', say so, and let me decide whether to give it.

author: hannah_w
body: Free speech and kindness aren't opposites. Most of us manage both before lunch.

author: hannah_w
body: The best philosophy is often hiding in children's books. 'Is it still my teddy if I've replaced all the stuffing?' is a problem Plutarch spent pages on.

author: hannah_w
body: Should voting be compulsory? Australia does it and turnout sits around 90%. I can't decide whether that's democracy working or democracy being nagged into the room.

author: hannah_w
body: Asked my students to write about ethics without using a chatbot. Three of them used a chatbot to ask how.

author: hannah_w
body: Thought experiments are experiments where the lab is your head and the budget is zero. Underrated research method.

author: rory_mck
body: Six Nations argument for the pub: Scotland's best rugby is played in the first 20 minutes and the last 10. The middle 50 is a mystery even to the coaches.

author: rory_mck
body: Cross-country is the most hated thing in PE and I think we've been doing it wrong. We send thirty kids round a muddy field and rank them, and the bottom ten learn they hate running forever. This term I let them run in pairs, at a pace where they can still talk, and stopped timing anyone who didn't want to be timed. Nobody broke a record. Half the class asked to do it again. I'll take that trade.

author: rory_mck
body: Rugby or football: which is Scotland's real national sport? Asking for a staffroom that hasn't spoken in two days.

author: rory_mck
body: Concussion rules in school rugby are much stricter than when I played, and good. I've seen kids sit out a game and come back fine. I've also known older players who never got that chance.

author: rory_mck
body: Borders rugby: muddy, freezing, and everyone's cousin is on the other team.

author: rory_mck
body: Parents' evening tip: if your child says PE is 'fine', it means they've been hiding in the changing room since September.

author: rory_mck
body: Grassroots rugby clubs are struggling because nobody wants to be the volunteer treasurer. If you can do a spreadsheet, your local club needs you more than it needs another prop.

author: zara_k
body: Tenants' union drop-in this week: a nursing student with mould up her bedroom wall, a family of four told to leave so the flat can be 'refurbished' and relet for more, and a pensioner whose rent has gone up three times in two years. None of them are unusual. People say rent control is radical. What's radical is a city where nurses can't afford to live near the hospital. I'd rather argue about the details of a cap than pretend this is fine.

author: zara_k
body: Short-term lets took whole stairs out of the housing market in the Old Town. You can be pro-tourism and still think homes should be homes.

author: zara_k
body: To every landlord who's told me 'I'm one of the good ones': great, then you won't mind the rules. Good landlords are the reason regulation is easy, not the reason it's unnecessary.

author: zara_k
body: Law school is half learning the law and half learning that you can't afford to practise the kind you went in for.

author: zara_k
body: Flat viewing today. 'Cosy' meant a bed in the kitchen.

author: zara_k
body: Know-your-rights reminder: your landlord can't just tell you to be out by the weekend. There's a written notice process. If something feels off, talk to a tenants' union or an advice service before you start packing.

author: zara_k
body: Protest songs are making a comeback at our union meetings. Mostly because someone brought a guitar and nobody had the heart to stop him.

author: zara_k
body: I disagree with Samuel's take on rent controls, but he's the only economist who's actually turned up to one of our meetings and listened for two hours. Respect where it's due.

author: kirsty_d
body: Running a small shop in this city is like being on a boat that's always slightly taking on water. Rent up again. Rates up again. Card fees nibbling at everything. Then a woman comes in for wool to finish the jumper her late husband never finished, and we spend forty minutes matching the colour, and I remember why I opened the door in the first place. It doesn't make the rent cheaper. It does make it worth it.

author: kirsty_d
body: Hearts fan in a Hibs-loving plumber's world. Ollie fixed my boiler last year and we've argued about football every time I've seen him since. Best customer relationship I have.

author: kirsty_d
body: 'Shop local' is lovely on a poster. It's lovelier on a rainy Tuesday when you need a birthday present and you walk past the internet to get it.

author: kirsty_d
body: Knitting is not a gentle hobby. It's maths, patience, and occasionally swearing at a cable pattern at midnight.

author: kirsty_d
body: Card fees ate my lunch budget this month. Literally.

author: kirsty_d
body: Result aside, the noise at Tynecastle when the teams come out still makes the hair on my arms stand up. Twenty-six years and it hasn't worn off.

author: kirsty_d
body: A customer asked if I could 'just knit something quick' for her dog by Friday. I admire the optimism.

author: theo_m
body: Indie game dev status: the lighthouse game now has a lighthouse. It doesn't light up yet. That's next month.

author: theo_m
body: Games are the most important art form nobody takes seriously. A novel can tell you about loneliness. A game can make you choose to walk away from someone, and then sit with the fact that you did. That's not a lesser kind of storytelling, it's a different kind, and we're still working out the grammar. I'm not saying every game is art. Most aren't. Most novels aren't either.

author: theo_m
body: Crunch is a management failure that gets described as passion. If your release date needs people sleeping under desks, the date was wrong.

author: theo_m
body: Researching lighthouses for the game and learned how many of Scotland's were built by one family of engineers. Generations of them putting towers on rocks in the sea, by hand, in storms. And I complain about merge conflicts.

author: theo_m
body: Playing a game set in Edinburgh. Already found three geography errors. Loving it anyway.

author: theo_m
body: Generative AI is genuinely useful for placeholder art and genuinely bad for final art. The trouble is how quietly placeholders become final.

author: theo_m
body: Board game night rule: whoever explains the rules isn't allowed to win the first game. It's the only way to keep friendships intact.

author: amara_j
body: Every few months a new 'protocol' goes round the running club. Cold plunges, morning sunlight, exact grams of protein per meal, magnesium before bed. Some of it might help a little. Most of it is a lot of effort for a small difference, and the people selling it rarely mention that part. My unglamorous routine: run, eat normal food, sleep, try not to get injured. It's not a podcast. It's got me through six marathons.

author: amara_j
body: Ran up Arthur's Seat for the first time. 'It's just a hill,' they said. It is a volcano with opinions.

author: amara_j
body: Running hasn't made me thin, fast or calm. It's made me someone who goes outside every day, which turns out to be the thing I needed.

author: amara_j
body: Ohio has flat. Edinburgh has hills, wind and cobbles. My knees have filed a formal complaint.

author: amara_j
body: Scottish tablet is just fudge that went to the gym.

author: amara_j
body: Parkrun at 9am on a Saturday in the rain is the most British thing I've ever done, and I've had tea with a vicar.

author: amara_j
body: Rest week. My body is thrilled. My brain keeps asking if we're sure.

author: noor_h
body: The New Town is a lesson in restraint. Same stone, same window proportions, street after street, and somehow it never feels monotonous. The variety is in the small things: a fanlight, a railing, the way the light hits a bay window at four in the afternoon. Damascus taught me to love ornament. Edinburgh is teaching me to love repetition done well. Both cities were built to outlast the people who built them.

author: noor_h
body: Architecture students: draw by hand at least sometimes. The computer tells you what's possible. The pencil tells you what you actually want.

author: noor_h
body: Too much new housing here is designed to be sold rather than lived in for thirty years. You can see it in the materials, the tiny windows, the balconies nobody can fit a chair on.

author: noor_h
body: Old Damascus houses were built around courtyards to stay cool in summer. Edinburgh tenements were built to keep you alive in winter. I live in a tenement and dream about courtyards.

author: noor_h
body: Brutalism is beautiful in the sun and devastating in the rain.

author: noor_h
body: My mother still posts me jars of apricot jam from home. Not one has ever gone missing. I suspect the postal service is afraid of my mother.

author: liam_oc
body: Delivery riding, honestly: I like the freedom and I like being outside. I don't like the app deciding my pay per drop and changing it without telling me, or the night I came off on black ice and lost two days of earnings while my wrist healed. People argue about whether we're employees or self-employed. I think we're a third thing nobody's written rules for yet, and until somebody does, all the risk sits with the person on the bike.

author: liam_oc
body: Celtic fan living in Edinburgh. It's lonely, but the pubs show the games and the Hibs lads are decent company as long as nobody mentions the 2010s.

author: liam_oc
body: Tipping in the app is lovely. Tipping in cash is lovelier. Just saying.

author: liam_oc
body: The best shortcuts in Edinburgh are known only to delivery riders and taxi drivers, and we will never tell you. Some secrets are professional.

author: liam_oc
body: If cycle lanes keep ending without warning at the exact spot the traffic gets worst, I'm going to start taking it personally.

author: liam_oc
body: Three things the app doesn't know: which stairs are lit, which dogs bite, and which customers come to the door in a dressing gown and say 'you're a star'. The last one is most of the job.

author: liam_oc
body: Five-a-side Thursday. I'm the oldest by six years and the only one who stretches. Coincidence? I think not.

author: ravi_p
body: As an actuary I'm professionally boring about risk, so here's the boring thought. A lot of money stress isn't about big decisions, it's about having no buffer. Even a small emergency pot, a few hundred pounds, turns a broken washing machine from a crisis into an annoyance. That's not investment advice, it's just maths about bad days. Bad days are guaranteed. Their size isn't.

author: ravi_p
body: The birthday problem still delights me. In a room of 23 people, there's a better than even chance two of them share a birthday. Most people guess you'd need well over a hundred.

author: ravi_p
body: Cricket stats are the best stats. Someone has recorded nearly every ball bowled in Test cricket since before your great-grandmother was born, and I find that deeply comforting.

author: ravi_p
body: Life expectancy figures describe populations, not people. 'Average' hides a huge spread, and the spread is where all the interesting stories are.

author: ravi_p
body: Risk isn't the opposite of safety. It's the price of anything interesting.

author: ravi_p
body: Spreadsheets are the most successful programming language nobody calls a programming language.

author: diego_v
body: Tacos in Scotland: I've tried every place that claims them. A few are good. One is great. Most are wraps with ambition.

author: diego_v
body: Startup ops is the job of making a company look like it has its act together while it's still assembling the act. Payroll, laptops, the office plant nobody waters, the contract someone signed in a café. I love it. But the honest truth about 'move fast' is that somebody has to come behind and tidy up, and that person is rarely in the funding announcement photo. Founders: thank your ops person this week. Bring snacks.

author: diego_v
body: Every startup I've worked at had the same five tools and the same argument about which one is the 'source of truth'. None of them are. The truth lives in the head of someone called Kevin.

author: diego_v
body: Unpopular opinion: open-plan offices are fine. What's not fine is open-plan offices with no quiet rooms and a manager who takes calls on speaker.

author: diego_v
body: Found proper corn tortillas in a shop in Leith. I may have cried a little.

author: diego_v
body: My mum in Guadalajara asked what time it gets dark here in winter. I said 'soon'. She said 'what time?' I said 'soon, and then sooner'.

author: gus_h
body: Allotment report: the leeks are magnificent, the brassicas have been eaten by something with ambition, and the man on plot 14 has built a shed nicer than my house.

author: gus_h
body: Wrote to the council again about the drain at the bottom of our street, which floods whenever it rains more than a little, which in Edinburgh is always. Fourth letter. I enclosed a diagram this time. Forty years as a civil engineer and I can tell you exactly what's wrong: the gully is too small for the area draining into it and the pipe has a dip where silt settles. They replied thanking me for my 'feedback'. I'll write again in spring.

author: gus_h
body: Leith Walk in 1972 and Leith Walk now are two different streets with the same name. Some things are better. The bakeries were better.

author: elena_d
body: Our choir sang a fifteenth-century piece last night in a church in Leith, to about thirty people. Someone wrote this music five hundred years ago for voices in a stone building, and the stone building still does what it was built to do: it holds the sound for a second after we stop. That second is why I sing. Nobody claps during it. Everyone just waits. I don't know another experience quite like that shared silence.

author: elena_d
body: Bulgarian folk music has time signatures like 7/8 and 11/16 that make classically trained musicians nervous. My grandmother danced to them all her life without counting once.

author: hamish_b
body: Diesel up again. Fertiliser up again. The price we get for barley about where it was five years ago. Farming is a long, slow lesson in things you can't control.

author: hamish_b
body: People ask what we grow. Barley for whisky, wheat for biscuits, potatoes for your chips. You've probably eaten a bit of my field.

author: hamish_b
body: Rain. Again. The ground is a sponge with a waiting list.

author: grace_t
body: Our branch library is on the 'review' list again. Here's what a review won't measure: the man who comes in every morning to read the paper because his flat is cold, the kids doing homework because there's no quiet at home, the woman we helped with a benefits form because the website kept timing out, and the rhyme time that's the only hour some new parents talk to another adult all week. We lend books too. That's honestly the least of it.

author: grace_t
body: Most borrowed book in our branch this month is a cookbook about soup. I'm choosing to read this as collective wisdom.

author: grace_t
body: Library confession: we can tell when you return a book you didn't read.

author: aroha
body: Moss appreciation post. Britain has well over a thousand species of moss and liverwort, and Scotland's west coast rainforest is one of the best places in Europe for them. They have no true roots, they take in water through their leaves, and some can dry out completely and spring back to life when it rains. I spent four hours yesterday on my knees in a wet gully in Argyll with a hand lens. Best day of my month.

author: aroha
body: Rotorua smells of sulphur and Argyll smells of wet leaves. I didn't expect to be homesick for the egg smell, but here we are.

author: wojtek
body: Rye sourdough needs four things: flour, water, salt, and someone stubborn enough to get up at 2am for it. I'm the fourth ingredient.

author: wojtek
body: 4am in the city: foxes, street sweepers, a couple arguing about who forgot the key, and me with flour in my eyebrows. The quietest, most honest hour.

author: wojtek
body: Pastel de nata, attempt number nine, because someone on here said nobody in Scotland gets them right. Tasted mine against her description. She has a point. Attempt ten tomorrow.

author: ama_s
body: Today in medieval marginalia: a scribe wrote, roughly, 'the ink is thin, the parchment is bad, the day is dark' in the margin of a gospel book. Eight hundred years later I feel this deeply.

author: ama_s
body: Thesis progress: chapter three exists. It has the shape of a chapter. It does not yet have the content of one.

author: jamie_lowe
body: Cramond at low tide this morning. Two curlews, a flock of knot moving like smoke, and a seal who looked at me like I owed it money.

author: jamie_lowe
body: The pink-footed geese are back for winter. Huge numbers come down from Iceland and Greenland to Scotland every autumn, and if you stand near a roost at dusk you hear them long before you see them, a noise like a crowd leaving a football match. They find their way over thousands of kilometres using the sun, the stars and probably things we haven't worked out yet. Twenty years watching and it still makes the back of my neck tingle.

author: jamie_lowe
body: Musselburgh lagoons are not glamorous. A car park, some ash, a hide with a broken latch. Also some of the best birding in the Lothians.

author: sunita_r
body: Maths teaching memory: a pupil once asked why we had to learn probability, so I asked him to work out his chances of being picked to answer the next question. He's an actuary now, apparently.

author: sunita_r
body: Chess club tonight. A nine-year-old beat me in twenty moves and then politely explained what I'd done wrong. I went home and set the board up again.

author: isla_r
body: Student climate activism gets painted as either heroic or annoying, and most of us are just tired. We do the marches, the petitions, the reading, and then go home to a rented flat with single glazing that costs a fortune to heat. I'd trade a lot of big speeches for a properly funded insulation scheme for rented homes. Not glamorous, but it cuts emissions and bills at the same time, which is the rare kind of policy nobody should have to fight about.

author: isla_r
body: Geography field trip to the Cairngorms. Snow in October, a ptarmigan, and a lecturer who got a bit emotional about a peat bog. Best week of the year.

author: isla_r
body: Is it just me or does the whole city catch a cold in the same week of October?

author: bea_s
body: Hi everyone, first post! I arrived from Porto Alegre four days ago and I've already been rained on, got lost on the way to campus twice, and been offered a cup of tea by a stranger at a bus stop. I think I'm going to like it here.

author: tariq_m
body: First post here. The hackathon starts tomorrow and I've already over-engineered our project in my head. Anyone else doing the backend for a team they haven't met yet?

author: freya_l
body: hello! not sure what to post first. my favourite thing about Edinburgh so far: the second-hand bookshops that smell like old churches.

author: oskar_j
body: Okay, first post. Cycled up the Royal Mile and nobody warned me about the cobbles. Dutch cycling did not prepare me for hills. Or cobbles. Or hills made of cobbles.
